summary:
Everyone though the Titanic was unsinkable until it sink 
but why did it sink ?
Because This "UNSINKABLE" was just concluded  by existing data

Same happened in Luna 25 & Chandrayan 2 was Well planned, prepared, experimented
but crashed 

Here, one common mistake in all three cases was relying mainly on existing data, past experiences, and static predictions to plan the missions. But they were not fully prepared to handle unexpected situations in real time, especially when communication was lost.

This is exactly where our solution comes in helping mission planners respond to any critical or emergency conditions and make better decisions in real time.
details:
MoonNav – Real-Time Lunar Mission Emergency Response and Recovery System

1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

MoonNav is an intelligent lunar mission decision-support platform designed to help mission planners evaluate unexpected emergency situations during lunar descent and landing, particularly in the challenging South Polar region.

Traditional mission planning relies heavily on pre-mission calculations, existing terrain datasets, predicted trajectories, and predefined operating procedures. However, unexpected events such as communication blackouts, trajectory deviations, excessive descent velocity, and unexpected terrain conditions can create situations where mission planners must rapidly evaluate alternative actions.

MoonNav aims to address this challenge through an interactive 3D lunar simulation and emergency-response decision-support system.

Our platform focuses on four major capabilities:

1. Communication Recovery Through Orbital Relays

If a lander loses direct communication with Earth because of terrain obstruction or unfavorable geometry, MoonNav evaluates whether a nearby communication-capable lunar orbiter or relay spacecraft could establish an alternative communication path.

The system visualizes the lander, Earth, orbital relay, and communication visibility in 3D. It evaluates whether the relay has simultaneous visibility to both the lander and Earth and identifies potential communication windows.

If direct communication is unavailable, the simulation can demonstrate an alternative communication pathway:

Lander → Orbital Relay → Earth.

2. Trajectory Deviation and Emergency Propulsion

If a lander travels beyond or falls short of its planned landing location, MoonNav simulates the deviation and evaluates possible recovery maneuvers.

For example, if excessive horizontal velocity causes an overshoot, the system evaluates whether a corrective retrograde thrust maneuver could reduce velocity. If the lander is descending too quickly, it evaluates whether sufficient braking capability remains.

Using configurable propulsion parameters, the simulator estimates the required velocity correction, fuel consumption, and recovery feasibility.

3. Visual Navigation and Terrain Awareness

In situations where communication or navigation information becomes unreliable, MoonNav explores the use of onboard camera-based visual navigation and terrain awareness.

The concept is to compare camera observations with available lunar terrain imagery and elevation information to help estimate the lander's position and identify surrounding terrain hazards.

This can help evaluate whether the lander is approaching an unsafe area and whether another landing location should be considered.

4. Alternative Landing Site Selection

If the original landing location becomes unreachable or unsafe, MoonNav evaluates alternative landing locations using terrain slope, surface characteristics, sunlight availability, Earth visibility, distance, and estimated maneuver feasibility.

It identifies potential alternatives and explains why a location may or may not be suitable.

The goal is to help mission planners compare possible recovery strategies instead of relying on a single predetermined landing plan.

2. What benefits does your project have?

  • Communication resilience: Explores alternative communication pathways when direct Earth communication is unavailable.
  • Emergency decision support: Helps evaluate possible responses to unexpected mission conditions.
  • Trajectory recovery: Simulates corrective propulsion maneuvers and estimates whether recovery is feasible.
  • Visual navigation: Explores camera-based position estimation and terrain awareness.
  • Alternative landing locations: Helps identify potentially reachable locations when the original target becomes unsuitable.
  • Improved mission awareness: Combines terrain, illumination, visibility, trajectory, and propulsion information in one interface.
  • Explainable decisions: Shows the assumptions, constraints, and reasons behind each suggested recovery option.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our intended impact is to move lunar landing mission planning beyond static pre-mission predictions toward more adaptive, contingency-aware decision support.

We want to help scientists and mission planners explore important questions:

  • What if communication with Earth is lost during descent?
  • Could an available orbital relay provide an alternative communication path?
  • What if the lander overshoots its intended landing location?
  • Is there enough remaining propulsion to perform a corrective maneuver?
  • What if the original landing location becomes unsafe?
  • Is there another reachable location with better terrain conditions?

By combining scientific datasets, geometric calculations, and interactive simulations, MoonNav aims to make emergency scenarios easier to understand and evaluate.

The long-term vision is to support safer, more resilient lunar exploration by helping mission teams examine unexpected situations and possible responses before and during mission operations.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

MoonNav is being developed as a web-based scientific visualization and decision-support application.

Software and development technologies:

  • TypeScript and JavaScript.
  • React and Next.js.
  • Web-based interactive 3D visualization.
  • PostgreSQL and Supabase for database and backend services.
  • Vercel for application deployment.
  • Scientific calculation and data-processing services.

Scientific and reference resources:

  1. NASA/ASU QuickMap: Lunar imagery, terrain visualization, and surface exploration.
    https://quickmap.lroc.asu.edu/
  2. NASA Moon Trek: Lunar elevation, slope, terrain, and surface analysis resources.
    https://trek.nasa.gov/moon/
  3. NASA JPL Horizons: Celestial-body ephemeris information for Sun and Earth positioning calculations.
    https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/
  4. Canadian Space Agency – Moon Exploration: Reference information about Gateway, Canadarm3, and future lunar exploration infrastructure.
    https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronomy/moon-exploration/

These resources contribute different types of information. Numerical calculations will use accessible, verifiable datasets and APIs where available. The CSA resource supports the explanation of future lunar infrastructure rather than providing live relay telemetry.

The prototype uses simulated spacecraft behaviour and configurable parameters for emergency scenarios. It does not require or claim access to operational spacecraft hardware.

5. How is your project creative?

The creative aspect of MoonNav is its focus on what happens when a lunar mission does not go according to plan.

Instead of only displaying where a lander should land, we explore what mission planners could do when conditions change unexpectedly.

Our interactive 3D environment allows users to trigger communication blackouts, observe orbital relay visibility, simulate trajectory deviations, evaluate corrective thrust maneuvers, and investigate alternative landing locations.

The system brings multiple emergency-response concepts together in a single visual environment.

For example, a user can simulate a lander losing direct communication, check whether an orbital relay can provide a possible communication path, observe an overshoot, evaluate whether corrective propulsion is sufficient, and investigate another landing site.

This combination of communication resilience, trajectory recovery, visual navigation, and alternative landing-site evaluation makes MoonNav more than a conventional lunar mapping tool.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We considered several important factors when designing MoonNav:

  • Communication limitations: Lunar terrain, Earth geometry, and relay visibility can affect communication opportunities.
  • Real-time uncertainty: Actual mission conditions may differ from pre-mission predictions.
  • Propulsion limitations: Corrective maneuvers depend on available thrust, remaining propellant, vehicle mass, and altitude.
  • Terrain safety: Slope, roughness, elevation, and local surface conditions affect landing suitability.
  • Lighting conditions: Solar illumination affects power opportunities and operational planning.
  • Navigation reliability: Camera-based terrain recognition and other navigation methods could provide additional information when available.
  • Scientific accuracy: We distinguish measured or retrieved scientific data from simulated parameters and assumptions.
  • Decision transparency: The system explains why a recovery option is feasible, infeasible, or uncertain.
